claims.claim: Eight different smart and feature phones ranging in price between ~$20 and ~$700 recorded quantitatively equivalent acoustic data from Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes.
claims.source: We compared eight different smart and feature phones ranging in price between ~$20 and ~$700 (Figure 2F), by analyzing 5 minutes of audio recorded with each phone from free-flying female Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes of similar age from a lab-reared population contained in a cage.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative recordings from multiple phone models.

claims.claim: Mean and median frequencies obtained by each phone differed by less than 5% from other phones for the same mosquito population.
claims.source: We noted high degrees of overlap in wingbeat frequency distributions recorded by each phone for this population, with both mean and median frequencies obtained by each phone differing by less than 5% from other phones (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the comparative data across different phone models.

claims.claim: The Bhattacharya Coefficient between phone pairs for the same mosquito population ranged between 0.93 and 1, indicating high degrees of overlap.
claims.source: We computed the Bhattacharya Coefficient (BC) and obtained high degrees of overlap between 0.93 and 1 (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the frequency distributions recorded by different phones.

claims.claim: The Jensen-Shannon divergence for each pair of phones had low values below 0.3, indicating high similarity in measurement.
claims.source: The JSD for each pair of phones had low values below 0.3 indicating high similarity in measurement, corroborating that wingbeat frequency sampling is relatively insensitive to the phone used.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the frequency distributions recorded by different phones.

claims.claim: A diverse range of both smart and feature phones provide highly similar acoustic spectra from the same population of mosquitoes.
claims.source: Thus, we demonstrate that a diverse range of both smart and feature phones provide highly similar acoustic spectra from the same population of mosquitoes, enabling a truly universal acoustics-based platform for mosquito identification.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the comparative analysis of recordings from multiple phone models.

claims.claim: Representative populations from 20 medically relevant mosquito species were surveyed under similar experimental conditions to establish a reference dataset.
claims.source: We surveyed representative populations from 20 medically relevant mosquito species under similar experimental conditions (Figure 3A), to establish a reference dataset for classifying acoustic recordings (Mukundarajan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is the experimental dataset collected and presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: A basic low-end phone (SGH T-209) is capable of collecting high-quality acoustic recordings to precisely measure wingbeat frequency distributions.
claims.source: Although we recorded mosquitoes using a variety of phones, the results presented here focus on data acquired by the 2006-model $20 SGH T-209 feature phone. This highlights that even a basic low-end phone is capable of collecting high-quality acoustic recordings, to precisely measure wingbeat frequency distributions.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the reference dataset collected using the T-209 phone.

claims.claim: A typical wingbeat frequency distribution for any given species has a spread of 150 to 200 Hz between the 5th and 95th percentiles.
claims.source: A typical wingbeat frequency distribution for any given species has a spread of 150 to 200 Hz between the 5th and 95th percentiles, located within the frequency range of 200 to 700 Hz for most female mosquitoes.
claims.evidence: This is observed from the frequency distribution data collected from 20 mosquito species.

claims.claim: Approximately 60 samples, or 1.2 seconds of recording time, is sufficient to generate a well-sampled wingbeat frequency distribution for a given population.
claims.source: The time for convergence above a BC of 0.9 corresponds to approximately 60 samples, or 1.2 seconds of recording time, to generate a well-sampled wingbeat frequency distribution for a given population.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the convergence analysis of bootstrapped subsets from reference distributions.

claims.claim: Different lab-reared strains of Anopheles gambiae produced highly similar frequency distributions with mutual Bhattacharya Coefficients of 0.84 to 0.89.
claims.source: We found that different lab-reared strains of An. gambiae, including permethrin susceptible and resistant variants sourced from Kenya and an additional bendiocarb resistant strain sourced from Benin, produced highly similar frequency distributions with large overlaps of 0.84 to 0.89 as measured by their mutual BCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative analysis of different An. gambiae strains.

claims.claim: Different colonies of Aedes aegypti had high overlaps in their frequency distributions with mutual Bhattacharya Coefficients ranging between 0.66 and 0.74.
claims.source: Similarly for Aedes aegypti, lab-reared mosquitoes from two separate colonies of the same New Orleans origin, as well as first generation progeny from eggs retrieved from the field in Los Angeles, had high overlaps in their frequency distributions with mutual BCs ranging between 0.66 and 0.74 (the slightly lower BC values arise due to the distribution for one of the colonies having a smaller spread despite being completely overlapped by the other two) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative analysis of different Ae. aegypti colonies.

claims.claim: Lab-reared strains of Anopheles arabiensis from Senegal and Sudan have non-overlapping frequency distributions with a Bhattacharya Coefficient of 0.14.
claims.source: However, we also found that lab-reared strains of An. arabiensis originally sourced from Senegal and Sudan have non-overlapping frequency distributions, with a very small BC of 0.14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative analysis of different An. arabiensis strains.

claims.claim: The vast majority of all possible pairwise combinations of species (184 out of 190) had Jensen-Shannon divergence greater than 0.35.
claims.source: The vast majority of all possible pairwise combinations of species in our study (184 out of 190) had JSD greater than this minimum value (Figure 3B), indicating that differences in frequency distribution between species are significant in most cases (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the pairwise comparisons of frequency distributions for 20 species.

claims.claim: Species with fairly unique and non-overlapping wingbeat frequency distributions are almost always correctly classified.
claims.source: Our results verify that species with fairly unique and non-overlapping wingbeat frequency distributions are almost always correctly classified, while those with high degrees of overlap are most likely to be mutually misclassified.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the confusion matrix analysis of bootstrapped data.

claims.claim: Including a location filter based on entomological survey data significantly improved classification accuracy from about 35% to 65% on average.
claims.source: This significantly improved classification accuracy not only for individual species, but also from about 35% to 65%, as an average over all the species tested (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the classification experiments with and without location filtering.

claims.claim: Anopheles gambiae and Culex pipiens can easily be distinguished by sound alone with negligible probability of mutual mis-classification.
claims.source: In the simplest case, species with completely non-overlapping frequency distributions, such as Anopheles gambiae and Culex pipiens (JSD = 1, negligible probability of mutual mis-classification), can easily be distinguished by sound alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the frequency distribution analysis and classification results.

claims.claim: Anopheles gambiae and Anopheles quadriannulatus are correctly identified with over 97% probability.
claims.source: The JSD for all but one species pair ranges between 0.61 and 0.91 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E), and An. gambiae and An. quadriannulatus are correctly identified with over 97% probability.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the classification analysis of the An. gambiae species complex.

claims.claim: Mosquito recordings with high SNR were obtained in a wide range of ambient environments, from urban and rural homes to forests and parks.
claims.source: We also collected recordings in a wide range of ambient environments, from urban and rural homes, both indoors and outdoors, to forests and parks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary files 2–7). We obtained mosquito recordings with high SNR, whose distinctive narrow-spectrum characteristics allow their easy visual identification in spectrograms against background noises such as birdsong, fire truck sirens, and human speech.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the field recordings collected in various environments.

claims.claim: For individual flight traces collected in the field, the frequency distributions have spreads between 10 and 100 Hz.
claims.source: For individual flight traces collected in the field, the distributions lie at different positions within the population-level frequency range, and have spreads (difference between 5th and 95th percentile) between 10 and 100 Hz (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This is observed from the analysis of individual Aedes sierrensis recordings from the field.

claims.claim: The spread in frequency for a single flight trace is typically smaller than the spread across a population.
claims.source: The spread in frequency for a single flight trace is typically smaller than the spread across a population, with the difference between mean frequencies for different traces contributing to the additional variation in the population's frequency distribution.
claims.evidence: This is observed from the comparative analysis of individual traces versus population distributions.

claims.claim: Frequency distributions for individual flight traces have a minimum spread of around 2% of the mean frequency irrespective of the mean frequency or the duration of the recording.
claims.source: We also observed that frequency distributions for individual flight traces have a minimum spread of around 2% of the mean frequency irrespective of the mean frequency or the duration of the recording, suggesting that this is an inherent natural variation in the wingbeat frequency during free flight (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is observed from the analysis of individual flight traces from wild Aedes sierrensis.

claims.claim: For mosquitoes varying almost two-fold in size, the difference in mean frequency between each mosquito is less than the spread within each individual flight trace.
claims.source: For mosquitoes varying almost two-fold in size (Figure 3G), the difference in mean frequency between each mosquito is less than the spread within each individual flight trace, and non-monotonic with body size (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the analysis of Aedes sierrensis specimens with varying body sizes.

claims.claim: The MLE approach correctly classified recordings from wild Aedes sierrensis mosquitoes in about two-thirds of cases (54 out of 82 recordings).
claims.source: Despite the variations among individuals, our MLE approach (using a pool of all field recordings together to create a reference frequency distribution) was able to correctly classify recordings from wild Aedes sierrensis mosquitoes in about two-thirds of cases (54 out of 82 recordings), when considering other local species (Cx. pipiens, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Cx. tarsalis, and Cu. incidens) as potential confounders.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the classification analysis of field recordings from Big Basin Park.

claims.claim: Recordings from Big Basin Redwoods State Park were collected over a continuous 3 hour period by 15 volunteers hiking along trails and recording with their personal mobile phones.
claims.source: These were collected over a continuous 3 hour period by 15 volunteers hiking along trails and recording with their personal mobile phones.
claims.evidence: This describes the field trial methodology at Big Basin Park.

claims.claim: About 60 recordings were collected in a 3-hour period by 10 volunteers at Ranomafana, Madagascar.
claims.source: About 60 recordings were collected in a 3-hour period by 10 volunteers who were trained for about 15 minutes and stationed at specific locations in the village.
claims.evidence: This describes the field trial methodology at Ranomafana.

claims.claim: The number of recordings at Ranomafana exceeded the number of mosquitoes simultaneously captured in CDC light traps placed at the same locations.
claims.source: This number of recordings exceeded the number of mosquitoes simultaneously captured in CDC light traps placed at the same locations.
claims.evidence: This is a direct comparison between mobile phone recordings and traditional trapping methods.

claims.claim: CDC light traps collected Anopheles mosquitoes only in those locations where they were also recorded by volunteers.
claims.source: This heterogeneity was concordant with the data from CDC light traps, which collected Anopheles mosquitoes only in those locations where they were also recorded by volunteers (Figure 4C, insets).
claims.evidence: This is observed from the comparison of mobile phone recordings and trap data at Ranomafana.

claims.claim: Wingbeat frequency for insects, including mosquitoes, has been shown to vary linearly with temperature.
claims.source: Wingbeat frequency for insects, including mosquitoes, has been shown to vary linearly with temperature (Oertli, 1989; Villarreal et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is cited from published literature on insect flight physiology.

claims.claim: Lab studies show no relationship between wingbeat frequency and body size.
claims.source: This provides a field confirmation of lab studies that show no relationship between wingbeat frequency and body size (Villarreal et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is cited from published literature and confirmed by field observations in this study.

results.result: Mobile phone microphones accurately capture mosquito wingbeat frequencies without distortion, as validated by synchronized audio-video recordings showing exact frequency matches within 2 Hz and a Bhattacharya Coefficient of 0.95 between audio and video measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 provide strong experimental validation through synchronized high-speed video and mobile phone audio recordings. The temporal alignment within 2 ms, frequency matching within 2 Hz, and BC of 0.95 demonstrate high fidelity acoustic capture. The experimental design with independent measurement modalities provides robust evidence.

results.result: Mobile phones, including decade-old feature phones, can detect mosquito wingbeat sounds at distances up to 50-100 mm with signal-to-noise ratios comparable to reference microphones, though performance is limited to environments with background noise below 50 dB.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 are supported by systematic calibration experiments using standardized sound sources and tethered mosquitoes. The distance measurements and SNR comparisons are quantitative and methodologically sound. The caveat about noise limitations (C36) appropriately qualifies the working conditions.

results.result: Eight different mobile phones ranging in price from ~$20 to ~$700 recorded quantitatively equivalent acoustic data from the same mosquito population, with mean/median frequencies differing by less than 5%, Bhattacharya Coefficients between 0.93-1, and Jensen-Shannon divergences below 0.3.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C41 demonstrate device-independence through systematic comparison of multiple phone models. The statistical metrics (BC, JSD) are appropriate for comparing distributions. The experimental design of recording the same population with different phones controls for biological variation. This is critical for establishing a universal platform.

results.result: A reference dataset of wingbeat frequency distributions was established for 20 medically relevant mosquito species using a low-cost feature phone, with typical distributions spanning 150-200 Hz and requiring approximately 1.2 seconds (60 samples) of recording for adequate sampling.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 describe the reference dataset construction with appropriate statistical validation. The convergence analysis (C45) using bootstrapping to determine adequate sample size is methodologically sound. Using the low-cost T-209 phone (C43) strengthens the accessibility argument. The dataset forms the foundation for classification.

results.result: Within-species variation in wingbeat frequency distributions was assessed across different strains and colonies, showing high similarity for most populations (BC 0.66-0.89) but notable exceptions like Anopheles arabiensis strains from different geographic origins (BC 0.14).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 appropriately characterize intraspecific variation with quantitative metrics. The finding of geographic variation in An. arabiensis (C48) is important for identifying limitations. However, the manuscript acknowledges this requires further investigation and recommends building local databases, which is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: Species classification using Maximum Likelihood Estimation achieved significant improvement from ~35% to ~65% average accuracy when incorporating location metadata as a filter, with 184 of 190 species pairs showing Jensen-Shannon divergence greater than 0.35.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 demonstrate the classification approach with appropriate statistical validation. The improvement from adding location metadata (C51) is substantial and well-documented. The JSD threshold of 0.35 is empirically derived from within-species variation. The confusion matrices provide transparent assessment of classification performance and limitations.

results.result: Specific species pairs demonstrate high classification accuracy, including Anopheles gambiae vs. Culex pipiens (negligible misclassification) and An. gambiae vs. An. quadriannulatus (>97% correct identification).
results.evaluation: Claims C53 and C57 provide specific examples of successful classification with quantitative probabilities. These are supported by the frequency distribution data and JSD calculations. The examples illustrate both the potential and limitations of acoustic classification for medically important species complexes.

results.result: Field recordings of wild Aedes sierrensis mosquitoes showed individual flight traces with frequency spreads of 10-100 Hz, typically smaller than population-level variation, with a minimum inherent spread of ~2% of mean frequency independent of recording duration or mosquito body size.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 characterize natural variation in field conditions with appropriate analysis. The finding that body size does not correlate with frequency (C63) is important and consistent with cited literature. The 2% minimum spread (C62) represents inherent biological variation. The high SNR recordings in diverse environments (C59) validate field applicability.

results.result: Field trials at Big Basin Redwoods State Park (15 volunteers, 3 hours) and Ranomafana, Madagascar (10 volunteers, 3 hours, ~60 recordings) demonstrated proof-of-concept for citizen science mosquito surveillance, with mobile phone recordings exceeding trap captures and showing concordant spatial patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 provide field validation with appropriate comparison to traditional methods (CDC light traps). The concordance between mobile recordings and trap data (C68) validates the approach. The classification accuracy of ~67% for wild Ae. sierrensis (C64) is reasonable given natural variation. The field trials demonstrate feasibility but are limited in scale and duration.

results.result: Mobile phones can be used as a platform for acoustic mosquito surveillance, with even low-cost devices capable of recording species-specific wingbeat sounds along with spatio-temporal metadata for rapid, non-invasive species identification by minimally-trained users.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C5, C6, and C21 represent the core thesis supported by the experimental validation throughout the manuscript. The technical validation (microphone performance, classification accuracy) and field demonstrations provide converging evidence. However, the system requires local reference databases and has limitations in noisy environments and for species with overlapping frequencies.

results.result: Current mosquito surveillance faces challenges due to paucity of high-resolution ecological data, with existing methods relying primarily on mathematical models rather than field surveys, and traditional methods requiring considerable expense, labor, and time.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C12 establish the motivation and context for the work, supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These are well-established challenges in the field of vector surveillance and disease control. The claims accurately represent the current state of mosquito monitoring.

results.result: Acoustic surveillance based on species-specific wingbeat frequencies was proposed decades ago but faced barriers to widespread adoption due to the challenge of using expensive microphones to acquire low-amplitude mosquito sounds against background noise.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 accurately summarize prior work on acoustic mosquito surveillance with appropriate historical citations. The characterization of technical barriers (C16) is well-supported by the cited literature and provides context for why mobile phones represent a novel solution.

results.result: The global mobile network connects ~5.3 billion users with 6% annual growth, with explosive growth most pronounced in Africa, Asia, and Latin America—regions that also bear the brunt of mosquito-borne diseases.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C20 provide factual statistics from cited reports that establish the infrastructure and geographic overlap supporting the proposed surveillance approach. The statistics are appropriately sourced and relevant to the feasibility argument.

results.result: Mosquito wingbeat sounds have relatively low acoustic complexity, comprising a fundamental frequency with overtones, showing natural frequency variations of 150-200 Hz for females (200-700 Hz range) that overlap with the voice frequency band where phones have maximum sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C24, C27-C29 characterize mosquito acoustic properties with data from 20 species. The spectral analysis is appropriate and the overlap with phone sensitivity (C29) is a key technical insight. The characterization of natural variation (C24) is important for understanding classification challenges.

results.result: Mobile phones automatically record time and location metadata and are optimized for sophisticated audio capture, processing, and transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C22 describe known capabilities of mobile phone technology. These are well-established features that support the metadata-enhanced classification approach. No experimental validation is needed for these general technology characteristics.

results.result: Wingbeat frequency varies linearly with temperature but shows no relationship with body size, as confirmed by field observations of wild mosquitoes.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 cite established literature on insect flight physiology and provide field confirmation for the body size relationship. The field data (C63) showing no correlation between frequency and two-fold size variation supports C70. Temperature effects (C69) are noted but not experimentally addressed in this study.
